title: Shortest paths in Java (PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque, int overflow)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Dijkstra with PriorityQueue and lazy deletion, comparator and overflow pitfalls, 0-1 BFS with ArrayDeque, Bellman-Ford for K stops and Floyd-Warshall with int[] tables.
source: Oracle Java PriorityQueue and ArrayDeque docs; JLS 4.2.2 (integer arithmetic) and 15.18; CLRS ch. 22-24; LeetCode Cheapest Flights Within K Stops, Network Delay Time

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int[] dijkstra(List<int[]>[] g, int n, int src)` where `g[u]` holds `{v, weight}` pairs with non-negative weights. Return the distance array (`Integer.MAX_VALUE` for unreachable nodes) using a `PriorityQueue<int[]>`.
questions.explanation: This is the lazy-deletion version: Java `PriorityQueue` has no decrease-key, so duplicates are pushed and stale ones skipped. Other correct variants (a `visited[]` array, a `Node` record) pass the intent. Time O(E log V). Note `d + e[1]` is safe because d is a popped, finite distance.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int cheapest(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k)` where each flight is `{from, to, price}`. Return the cheapest price using at most k stops, or -1 if impossible. Use Bellman-Ford rounds and avoid int overflow when adding to an 'infinite' distance.
questions.explanation: The clone matters: relaxing in place could chain several edges in one round and exceed the K-stop limit. `Integer.MAX_VALUE / 2` plus a price cannot overflow, unlike `Integer.MAX_VALUE + price`. Time O(K * E). A heap-based search tracking (cost, node, stops) is also valid but would not satisfy these checks.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int[][] floyd(int[][] dist)` that updates an n x n matrix in place to all-pairs shortest distances and returns it. Missing edges hold `INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE / 2` and the diagonal holds 0.
questions.explanation: O(n^3) time, O(1) extra space. The intermediate vertex k must be the outer loop. Using `INF = MAX_VALUE / 2` keeps `INF + INF` from overflowing. It suits small dense graphs; for large sparse graphs run Dijkstra from each source.

checks.label: tests a path through the middle vertex

questions.prompt: Directed edges A->B 4, A->C 1, C->B 2, C->D 8, B->D 5, D->E 3. Dijkstra from A uses a `PriorityQueue` with lazy deletion: one add for the source, then one add per successful relaxation. How many times is add called in total?
questions.explanation: Source (1), A relaxes B and C (3), C relaxes B to 3 and D to 9 (5), B relaxes D to 8 (6), D relaxes E (7). The stale entries (4,B) and (9,D) are popped and skipped. In general pushes are at most E + 1.

questions.prompt: Distances in a `PriorityQueue<int[]>` may be close to 2 billion, and entries are ordered by `a[0]` ascending. Which comparator is always correct?
questions.explanation: Subtraction comparators are a classic overflow bug. `Integer.compare`, `Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0])` or `Long.compare` for long keys are safe.

options.why: Correct: compare never overflows and returns the right sign.

options.text: `(a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]`, which wraps around when the two values are far apart
options.why: The subtraction can overflow int and flip the sign, corrupting the heap order.

options.text: `(a, b) -> b[0] - a[0]`, so that the larger distance leaves the heap first
options.why: This reverses the order, giving a max-heap, and also risks overflow.

options.text: No comparator at all, because `int[]` arrays are naturally ordered by their first element
options.why: Arrays do not implement `Comparable`; the first add throws `ClassCastException`.

questions.prompt: True or false: `PriorityQueue.remove(Object)` runs in O(log n), so Dijkstra can simulate decrease-key by removing the old entry and adding the new one at no real cost.
questions.explanation: `PriorityQueue.remove(Object)` scans the backing array, then sifts. Lazy deletion (add a duplicate, skip stale on `poll`) keeps every operation O(log n).

options.why: `remove(Object)` first searches for the element, which is linear in the heap size.
Correct: the search makes `remove(Object)` O(n), so the trick turns Dijkstra into O(V * E) work.

questions.prompt: Complete the Java container choice for 0-1 BFS.
questions.explanation: `ArrayDeque` is the idiomatic double-ended queue in Java (faster than `LinkedList` and `Stack`). Front insertion for free moves keeps the deque ordered by distance, giving O(V + E).
questions.text: 0-1 BFS keeps its frontier in an {1}: a neighbour reached by a weight-0 edge goes in with {2}, one reached by a weight-1 edge goes in with {3}.

questions.prompt: A developer prints a `PriorityQueue<Integer>` of the values 5, 1, 4, 2 with a for-each loop.
questions.explanation: To read in order, `poll` repeatedly (O(log n) each) or copy and sort. The iterator walks the underlying array in heap order.
questions.assertion: Iterating a `PriorityQueue` with a for-each loop visits the elements in ascending order.
questions.reason: A `PriorityQueue` is a binary heap in an array, which only guarantees that the head is the minimum.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.c: A is false, and R is true.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is exactly why A is false; only poll() returns elements in sorted order.

questions.prompt: You write `new PriorityQueue<int[]>()` and add two `int[]` entries.
questions.explanation: Always pass a comparator for array or custom-object entries, for example `Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0])`.
questions.reason: `int[]` arrays implement `Comparable`, ordering themselves by their first element.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: arrays are not Comparable, so without a comparator the second add throws ClassCastException; A is true and R is false.

questions.explanation: Both facts feed the Dijkstra bound: up to E polls at O(log V) each, with peek used only for inspection.

whys.a: Peek being O(1) does not explain why poll must sift.
whys.b: Right: both are true; poll must restore the heap by sifting, while peek just reads the head, and neither explains the other.

questions.prompt: A student fills `dist` with `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and relaxes edges with `dist[u] + w < dist[v]` without checking reachability.
questions.explanation: Fix it by skipping unreachable nodes, using `long`, or choosing `INF = MAX_VALUE / 2`. Dijkstra avoids the problem because it only relaxes from popped, finite nodes.
questions.assertion: Using `Integer.MAX_VALUE` as infinity can break relaxation for an unreachable u.
questions.reason: Adding a positive weight to `Integer.MAX_VALUE` wraps around to a negative int.

whys.a: Right: the wrapped negative sum looks smaller than dist[v], so a bogus distance is stored.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A.

questions.prompt: Match each shortest-path need with the Java construct that fits it.
questions.explanation: BFS needs FIFO (`ArrayDeque`), Dijkstra a min-heap, 0-1 BFS both ends of a deque. Switch to `long` when sums can pass `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. `Stack` is a legacy LIFO class and not a queue.

questions.prompt: After polling `{d, u}` from the `PriorityQueue` in lazy-deletion Dijkstra, which check prevents redoing work for outdated entries?
questions.explanation: Without the check the algorithm stays correct but can re-expand a node many times, degrading toward O(V * E) on dense graphs.

options.why: This skips exactly the valid entries and keeps the stale ones.
Correct: a larger d than the recorded best means a better entry was already processed.
`contains` is linear and compares the wrong thing, an `int[]` by reference.
A polled node always has a finite distance, so this never triggers.
